speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IDA is the arm of the World Bank Group that provides grants and concessional loans to its least developed member countries, including some of our ASEAN neighbours like Laos and Cambodia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore has contributed to IDA’s replenishments since 2002.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This 13% increase makes it the largest financing envelope in IDA’s history; and demonstrates solidarity by both developed and developing countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As highlighted by my colleague Senior Minister of State for Finance, Mr Chee Hong Tat, when he moved the Second Reading of the IDA (Amendment) Bill last October, as a responsible member of the international community, Singapore will do our part.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: During our early days, Singapore had benefited from loans and expertise from the World Bank to build key infrastructure as part of our nation-building efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We remember and are grateful for this assistance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are in a better position today; but we know from experience the challenges developing countries face and we want to play our part and give back.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are also positive benefits in working with marquee institutions like the World Bank Group.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This contribute to Singapore’s place as an infrastructure financing hub for the development of our region.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It also creates good opportunities for Singaporeans and Singapore-based companies as the region prospers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will translate to a subscription of no more than US$70 million.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Funding rounds for the International Development Association either are similar and occur every three years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Motion before us today is to provide said funding for IDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my earlier contribution to the IMF Motion, I had made the case for why contributing to international development efforts can benefit us by enhancing our hard and soft power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And why doing so even when it does not remain a moral imperative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have also made the case for why we should systematised official development assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, I will elaborate on both of these themes and in particular made a more pointed case for a specialised Singaporean foreign aid agency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I had previously shared, I have worked for seven years at the World Bank Group in the past of which either as a part and during my tenure at the bank, I have contributed to the work of IDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I also have a small balance in my self-funded group retirement account and a staff account at the Credit Union, but do not currently receive nor maintain any direct financial interest in the bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the pandemic is largely a matter of the past for us and we have more or less successfully transition to treating COVID-19 as an endemic disease, the ravages of COVID remain very real in other parts of the world, especially in the poorest economies of Africa, as well as Asia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This anaemic growth in our neighbours will affect us too because while Singapore's growth rebounded strongly in 2021 and remain solid last year, it is expected to falter this year in part because of tighter monetary conditions worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In our assistance to our neighbours and major trade partners helps spark better economic conditions in those places.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We could enjoy the spill-over effects from their belated recoveries which could in turn offer a neat counterbalance to weakening conditions in advanced economies worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has also enhanced its post-pandemic soft power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Members of this House, including those of the Workers' Party, have flagged certain refinements to our approach assessments of our overall pandemic response and subsequent reopening, have on net been positive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, according to an index developed by the University of Southern California, the weakest aspect of Singapore's soft power remains our international engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Enhancing our foreign aid profile can, therefore, further bolster our outreach to our neighbours and improve our foreign relations accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, IDA and the World Bank remain among the most effective, transparent and development-focused institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we were to decide that it is a good idea to channel financial support to multilateral development agencies, we can do far worse than doing so through IDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But even multilateral agencies that have a solid reputation for largely unbiased foreign aid practices may end up inadvertently being subject to quid pro quo exchanges, especially between large players.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, while there is solid reason to support development in the poorest nations globally, the nature of multilateral development agencies is that their support is not solely targeted at countries in Southeast Asia, which is our immediate neighbourhood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We wish to have more directed support in a manner that could potentially spill over onto our shores.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is why I wish to go a step further and explain why it s also in our interest to form a small but dedicated foreign aid agency, much like how we already appropriate development funds for various longer-term financial commitments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, to the extent that we already have civil servants within MFA, whose work is mainly focused on external finance and economic relations, we can hive them off to this new agency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can supplement this professional team with a stream of rotational staff and interns, especially those who have an interest or experience with international economics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, we can second MFA staffers who deal with international economic relations to this body and then absorb a small number of university interns annually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over time, the agency can even be an oversight body that allows us to launch, perhaps an international volunteer corps – another initiative that I had previously advocated for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One concern that some may have about bilateral development agencies of this nature is how they may become tools of foreign policy and consequently the aid offered becomes ineffective at best, or could even end up harming the countries it purports to assist at worst.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can pre-empt such concerns in a few ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, as I have already alluded to, we can keep the agency's mandate narrow and budget tight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will keep the body focused on its core principles and discourage adventurism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, if we believe more in our ability to insulate such an agency from political interference than we do others, especially multilateral institutions a homegrown institution may be an even more efficient way to deliver official development assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I see little reason why we would run the proposed SingAid without the same technocratic vigour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Third, perhaps most importantly, our foreign policy interests are, by and large, largely remarkably neutral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is an ethos in fact for our entire Public Service and I see no reason why we cannot infuse such principles into a nascent aid agency that is likewise imbued with the same set of principles and avoids the risk that the body descends into becoming a geopolitical tool.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All that said, Mr Speaker, it should come as no surprise that I am in thorough support of the Motion and wish that it in fact goes a little further.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Listening to Assoc Prof Lim, I think there is in fact common ground and then there is a part where, perhaps, we have a slight difference of views.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The common ground is: is it a good thing to do, to do something to help developing countries?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Is it common ground that doing so would benefit countries in the region?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I think also that insofar as this specific Motion is concerned, since Assoc Prof Lim has given his support, I think we can take it that he is in agreement and that this particular issue can be put to rest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the only question is, do we do more?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if we do more, the question is to what extent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And what the Assoc Prof would like us to do is also to set up a foreign development aid agency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think he even has thought of a name for it. "SingAid" – that was the name he attributed to it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is where the differences are – which is how much more and do you set up an agency for this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the question of whether we should do more – and I think if I heard the Member correctly, he also talked about systematising it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If I remember correctly, that was the word he used.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first thing I should do is to assure the Chamber and others that contributing to IDA or the World Bank Group is not the only thing that we do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What we do is we take a balanced approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We look at what is commensurate with Singapore's size and we enter into obligations that we can afford over the long run, after the needs of Singaporeans are met.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When we look at international contributions, we do more than just contribute to the World Bank Group.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have actually done so through various other institutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that, in a way, takes care of the suggestion that it should be done in an institutionalised way, because what we are really doing is leveraging the systems, the administration, the infrastructure and the reach of such international institutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also contributed vaccines to our neighbours as part of our commitment to tide through the pandemic collectively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More recently, Singapore became a founding member of the Pandemic Fund to enhance global pandemic prevention, preparedness and response.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And late last year, we announced a sustainability action package at COP27, to support the capacity building needs of fellow developing countries on sustainability and climate issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, you can see that, firstly, we do work with and through institutions to amplify our reach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We go over and beyond that and we make direct contributions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But all of this is part and parcel of a balanced approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a small country, our resources are limited and we have to make sure that every dollar counts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will prioritise the needs of Singapore and Singaporeans; and use prudent fiscal management to manage our resources well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This allows us to grow the funds and there will be then space for us to contribute to the common good.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this is what we have done and this is what we will continue to do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also do not take our international financial obligations lightly as they often have long durations, and we cannot always predict what economic conditions will be like and what our fiscal situation will be like.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if you set up a development agency, that is a very long-term commitment and you need to be sure that you can carry this through.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Whilst I appreciate the sentiment within the Member's suggestion, one should also be mindful that we are a small country, we are constrained, we have limited resources.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, our approach is, look after our people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We give through institutions, we give directly, and we maintain some, so that we can be nimble and flexible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We must also be realistic to understand with our small size, exactly how much we can do by ourselves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is much that we can and should do, but we cannot do everything alone.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And working with others allows us to amplify the impact of what we do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But, that said, I thank the Member for his support.
